text.p: Most metals edged lower in thin holiday trade on Friday, with nickel falling to fresh 2-1/4 year lows and copper also lower after reversing some early gains.
Precious metals were flat to weaker, but oil prices rose on news of stock rundowns.
The CRB index ended down 1.82 points at 240.06.

Copper jerked lower in thin holiday trade on Friday afternoon after failing to hold firmer levels and most of the other metals moved in tandem. Three month copper prices took a quick look at a high of $2,165 per tonne in the morning, but were unable to sustain the upside momentum and drifted lower.

A breach of $2,150 after lunch triggered some sell-stops and prices lurched lower, ending the afternoon kerb with a loss of $17 at $2,127. The premium of cash over three months metal also softened from $105 in the morning to $95/$100 by the afternoon close. Support is pegged at $2,120/25, then at $2,077/80.

No LME stocks data were released on Friday due to the holidays. The next inventory report scheduled for Tuesday, when traders will be concentrating on copper levels in Singapore after the last report showed a delivery of 4,100 tonnes.

Aluminium also rose in the morning, peaking at $1,570 resistance before falling back to end the day at $1,546, down $11. Analysts said aluminium needed to break back above the up trend line, which was at $1,563 on Friday. Support is seen at $1,540, then at $1,506/7.

Nickel edged down to a fresh 2-1/4 year low of $6,476 and ended there, suffering a $4 loss. Analysts say the damaged technical picture makes more weakness likely, with targets of $6,340 and $6,200 expected.

Tin shed $50 to $5,730, descending back towards a 19-month low of $5,680 hit on December 16. Lead lost $6 to $713 but zinc bucked the trend and finished $3 higher at $1,075 after peaking at $1,080, the highest since November 27. Alloy ended weaker at $1,385/90 after $1,398.

New York precious metals futures ended flat to weaker in thin, featurelss holiday week trading. The precious metals complex largely ignored a sharp dip in November U.S. durable goods orders. The U.S. Commerce Department said orders in that month were off 1.6 percent in contrast to analysts' expectations of a modest 0.1 percent rise. The dollar's brief surge to a 44-month high of 116.20 yen also failed to excite the torpid yellow metal market.

COMEX February gold settled unchanged at $371.10 an ounce, traded narrowly between $371.70 and $370.80. Over-the-counter options in gold and silver expired 0930 EST, which prompted one fund to cover its short position in silver, a dealer said. "Even after the expiry, there was some good buying interest in the silver for most of the day," the dealer added.

London bullion market reopened Friday after a two-day Christmas break, but trading was sluggish and rangebound. Mid-afternoon New York bullion was quoted at $369.20/$369.70 an ounce, off the morning's high of above $370.00.

The NYMEX oil complex ended higher Friday after weekly oil inventory data showed bullish draws in crude and distillate stocks when traders had expected stock increases. "Prices started out higher, and they stayed there. The APIs were pretty much the story," said Al Lindseth, manager of oil and gas hedge programs at GSC Energy in Atlanta.

February crude ended up 30 cents at $25.22 a barrel. Jan heating oil ended up 0.49 cent a gallon at 70.55 cents. Jan gasoline ended up 0.23 cent a gallon at 69.74 cents. Volume was thin as traders extended the Christmas holiday through the week.

On Thursday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed a draw of 1.89 million barrels in distillate stocks for the week ended December 20. Distillate stocks are comprised of heating oil and diesel. Crude stocks fell 5.16 million barrels while gasoline stocks grew 504,000 barrels.

The U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Energy Information Administration (EIA) showed a draw of 300,000 barrels in gasoline stocks in its own weekly inventory data Thursday, as well as draws in distillate and crude.

Fresh buying and short-covering by the funds lifted CSCE world sugar futures sharply higher and over nearby resistance seen at 10.89 cents in March, dealers said. The trade stood on the opposite side of the market led by the producers, who were cited as steady scale-up sellers. One dealer said between 300 to 500 lots were probably sold from 10.84 at each tick higher.
"What it came to is steady fund buying, which gradually eroded scale-up selling," he said. "It was like a diagonal line: a very steady ascent reaching 10.90 on close."

The most-active March contract finished on resistance at 10.89, up 0.16, traded 10.90 to 10.73. The back months settled 0.16 to 0.11 firmer. Volume was estimated at 20,856 lots, which included 966 against actuals in March.

CBOT wheat futures closed lower with the market pressured late by small-lot fund selling amid a near dearth of buying interest, traders said. "O'Brien, Man, and CIS sold it late, it was just some fund liquidation. There was just nothing else in here," a trader said.

Traders said forecasts for weather considered conducive for the U.S. winter wheat crop may have hit the market. Wheat early was supported by export numbers but even that data failed to stir substantial bullish momentum.
USDA Friday said U.S. net export sales of wheat during the week ended December 19 totaled 353,200 tonnes, above the range of trade estimates for 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes.

There also were diminished fears about wet-weather related losses in Argentina's wheat growing region. However, traders in Buenos Aires said Argentine cash wheat was firm early Friday on forecasts for rain this weekend in key southern grain areas, which could lead to harvest delays.

Wheat closed unchanged to 4-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with March down 4-1/2 at $3.89-1/2. Wheat futures volume was estimated at 6,000 contracts, about the same as the 6,059 traded Thursday, according to the CBOT.
